blocks.text: Input validation checks whether incoming input conforms to expected constraints before any real processing happens, rejecting what falls outside those bounds entirely, a distinct security layer from prompt sanitization, covered in the previous topic, which cleans content rather than rejecting it.

This topic covers the difference between validation and sanitization, length and format checks, rejecting input outside expected bounds, detecting abuse patterns, and why validation belongs at the system boundary rather than scattered throughout deeper application logic.
1. Input Validation as a Security Gate

blocks.alt: Building on prompt sanitization, input validation acts as a security gate at the boundary

blocks.text: Input validation is a check that happens before any real processing, confirming that incoming input actually conforms to expected constraints, length, format, type, and rejecting anything that does not meet those constraints, rather than attempting to process it.
2. Validation vs Sanitization

blocks.alt: Validation rejects input outside bounds, sanitization cleans input to make it safer

blocks.text: This connects directly to the previous topic, sanitization takes potentially risky content and cleans it to make it safer to use, validation takes input and simply decides whether to accept or reject it outright based on whether it conforms to expected constraints, the two are complementary, not interchangeable.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","What It Does"],"rows":[["Sanitization","Cleans or transforms content to reduce risk"],["Validation","Accepts or rejects input based on expected constraints"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Length and Size Limits

blocks.alt: Input exceeding a length limit gets rejected outright

blocks.text: This connects directly to context window optimization, covered in an earlier module, an input far exceeding any reasonable expected length is both a potential resource abuse concern and often a signal something unusual, possibly malicious, is being attempted, rejecting oversized input before processing avoids both problems at once.
4. Format and Type Validation

blocks.alt: Expected format or type gets checked against whether the input actually matches it

blocks.text: This connects directly to structured outputs and schema-based outputs, both covered in an earlier module, but applied here to input rather than output, confirming an input field is actually the expected type, a number where a number is expected, a value from an expected set of options, catches malformed or unexpected input before it ever reaches a prompt.
5. Rejecting Input Outside Expected Bounds

blocks.alt: Input outside expected bounds gets rejected before any processing

blocks.text: Beyond length and format, validation can check whether input values fall within reasonable expected bounds for the specific application, a quantity field that should never be negative, a date field that should never be far in the past or future, rejecting values outside these bounds before they ever influence a prompt.
6. Detecting Abuse Patterns

blocks.alt: Unusual request volume or pattern gets flagged as a possible abuse pattern

blocks.text: At a broader level, validation can also include monitoring request patterns themselves, an unusual volume of requests from one source, or a pattern of requests that looks like automated probing for vulnerabilities, this connects to security testing and red teaming, covered later in this module, from the defensive monitoring side.

blocks.title: This connects to broader application security practice beyond just prompts
blocks.content: Rate limiting and abuse pattern detection are standard practices across web application security generally, applying them to an AI system endpoint follows the same well established principle, protecting against volume based abuse alongside content based attacks.

blocks.text: 7. Validation at the System Boundary

blocks.alt: Validation at the system boundary is compared against validation scattered deep inside application logic

blocks.text: Input validation works best applied consistently at the point where external input first enters a system, rather than scattered inconsistently throughout deeper application logic, a boundary check ensures every single request passes through the same consistent gate, rather than relying on validation happening correctly somewhere further downstream.
8. A Worked Input Validation Example

An application accepting a user question for a RAG system, covered in an earlier module, validates that the question is under a reasonable length limit, contains only expected character types, and does not exceed a per-user rate limit, rejecting anything outside these bounds before the question ever reaches the actual retrieval and prompt construction pipeline.
9. Input Validation and Output Validation, Revisited

This connects directly to output validation, covered in an earlier module, the two form a matched pair, checking what comes in before it gets used, and checking what comes out before it gets trusted, a genuinely secure and reliable system needs validation on both sides of the model, not just one.
Worked Example

A team building a customer service chat endpoint discovers an unusually large volume of extremely long messages arriving from a small number of sources, far exceeding any realistic legitimate customer message length, investigation reveals this is an automated attempt to probe for prompt injection vulnerabilities through brute force variation.

Adding a length limit and a per-source rate limit at the system boundary, rejecting outlier requests before they ever reach the actual model prompt, both blocks the immediate probing pattern and reduces the overall attack surface the team has to defend against with sanitization and other downstream techniques.
Common Mistakes

items: Relying on sanitization alone without also validating and rejecting input that falls clearly outside expected bounds
Scattering validation checks inconsistently throughout deep application logic instead of enforcing them at the system boundary
Not setting any length or rate limit, leaving a system open to resource abuse or automated probing
Validating format and type but ignoring reasonable bounds checks for the actual values within that format

blocks.text: Practice

Take an input field for an application you have built or could build, define explicit length, format, and reasonable value bounds for it, write a validation function enforcing all three, and test it against input deliberately crafted to violate each specific constraint.
Key Takeaway

Input validation checks incoming input against expected length, format, and value bounds, rejecting anything outside them before any real processing happens, complementary to sanitization rather than a replacement for it, and it works best enforced consistently at the system boundary alongside the output validation already covered in an earlier module.
